

```{r}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(spData)
library(spDataLarge)
library(sf)
library(stars)
library(terra)
library(tmap)
```


```{r}
dem <- terra::rast(system.file("raster/dem.tif", package = "spDataLarge"))
landsat <- terra::rast(system.file("raster/landsat.tif", package = "spDataLarge"))
srtm <- terra::rast(system.file("raster/srtm.tif", package = "spDataLarge"))
```

## Explore elevation at Mt. Mongón, Perú

Make a boxplot and histogram of elevation at Mt. Mongón, Perú
```{r}
hist(dem,
     main = 'Digital Elevation Model Distribution',
     xlab = 'Value')


boxplot(dem,
        main = 'Digital Elevation Model Distribution',
        ylab = 'Value')
```

Reclassify dem and compute the mean for the three classes:
- Low, where elevation is less than 300
- Medium
- High, where elevation is greater than 500

```{r}
# What I did:

# create reclassification matrix
rcl_dem <- matrix(c(0, 300, 1, 
                    300, 500, 2,
                    500, 1500, 3),
                    ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# use reclassification matrix to reclassify elevation raster
reclass_dem <- classify(dem, rcl = rcl_dem)

# change reclassified values into factors
values(reclass_dem) <- as.factor(values(reclass_dem))

# visualize
map1 <- tm_shape(dem) + 
    tm_raster(col.legend = tm_legend(title = 'Elevation')) +
    tm_title(text = "Original")

map2 <- tm_shape(reclass_dem) +
    tm_raster(col.legend = tm_legend(title = 'Elevation')) +
    tm_title(text = "Reclassified")

tmap_arrange(map1, map2, nrow = 1)

# Lab solution:

# Define a reclassification matrix
rcl <- matrix(c(-Inf, 300, 0, # values -Inf to 300 = 0
                300, 500, 1,  # values 300 to 500 = 1
                500, Inf, 2), # values 500 to Inf = 2
              ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# Apply the matrix to reclassify the raster, making all cells 0 or 1 or 2
dem_rcl <- terra::classify(dem, rcl = rcl)

# Assign labels to the numerical categories
levels(dem_rcl) <- tibble::tibble(id = 0:2, 
                                  cats = c("low", "medium", "high"))

# Calculate mean elevation for each category using original DEM values
elevation_mean <- terra::zonal(dem, dem_rcl, fun = "mean")
elevation_mean

# My add on - visualizing

values(dem_rcl) <- as.factor(values(dem_rcl))

map3 <- tm_shape(dem_rcl) +
    tm_raster(col.legend = tm_legend(title = 'Elevation')) +
    tm_title(text = "Reclassified lab solution")

tmap_arrange(map1, map3, nrow = 1)

```

## Explore NDVI and NDWI at Zion National Park
First, correct the scale across all grid cells and then apply the following functions at each grid cell:

NDWI = (green-NIR) / (green+NIR)
 
NDVI = (NIR-red) /  (NIR+red)

Calculate the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) at Zion National Park
Calculate the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) at Zion National Park
Find a correlation between NDVI and NDWI at Zion National Park


```{r}
scale_factor <- 0.0000275
offset <- 0.2


scale_function <- function(x) {
  x * scale_factor + offset
}

landsat_scaled <- terra::app(landsat, fun = scale_function)

ndwi_fun <- function(green, nir){
    (green - nir) / (green + nir)
}

ndvi_fun <- function(nir, red){
    (nir - red) / (nir + red)
}

ndwi_rast <- terra::lapp(landsat_scaled[[c(2,4)]], fun = ndwi_fun)

ndvi_rast <- terra::lapp(landsat_scaled[[c(4,3)]], fun = ndvi_fun)

plot(ndwi_rast, main = "Zion National Park NDWI")

plot(ndvi_rast,
     main = "Zion National Park NDVI")

combine <- c(ndvi_rast, ndwi_rast) # Stack rasters
plot(combine, main = c("NDVI", "NDWI"))

# Calculate correlation between raster layers 
terra::layerCor(combine, fun = cor)
```

## Change resolution of elevation at Zion National Park 

Use all the methods available to change the resolution of elevation at Zion National Park to 0.01 by 0.01 degrees
Note: The srtm raster has a resolution of 0.00083 by 0.00083 degrees

```{r}
plot(srtm)

rast_template <- terra::rast(terra::ext(srtm), res = 0.01) # Create empty template

srtm_resampl1 <- terra::resample(srtm, y = rast_template, method = "bilinear")
srtm_resampl2 <- terra::resample(srtm, y = rast_template, method = "near")
srtm_resampl3 <- terra::resample(srtm, y = rast_template, method = "cubic")
srtm_resampl4 <- terra::resample(srtm, y = rast_template, method = "cubicspline")
srtm_resampl5 <- terra::resample(srtm, y = rast_template, method = "lanczos")

srtm_resampl_all <- c(srtm_resampl1, srtm_resampl2, srtm_resampl3, srtm_resampl4, srtm_resampl5)
labs <- c("Bilinear", "Near", "Cubic", "Cubic Spline", "Lanczos")

plot(srtm_resampl_all, main = labs)
```

## Explore elevation at Mt. Mongon Peru 


```{r}
# Extract the array of values from the first (and only) attribute
dem_values <- as.vector(dem[[1]])

hist(dem_values,
     main = "Digital Elevation Model Distribution",
     xlab = "Value")
```


```{r}
boxplot(dem_values,
        main = "Digital Elevation Model Distribution",
        ylab = "Value")
```


```{r}
# Reclassify by cutting values into intervals, returning a factor raster
dem_rcl <- cut(dem,
               breaks = c(-Inf, 300, 500, Inf), # -Inf to 300, 300 to 500, 500 to Inf
               labels = c("low", "medium", "high"))

plot(dem_rcl, main = "Reclassified elevation")
```


```{r}
# Calculate mean elevation for each category using original DEM values
elevation_mean <- tibble(elevation = as.vector(dem[[1]]),
                         cats = factor(as.vector(dem_rcl[[1]]), levels = levels(dem_rcl[[1]]))) %>%
  group_by(cats) %>%
  summarise(mean_elevation = mean(elevation, na.rm = TRUE))
elevation_mean
```


```{r}
# Polygonize the reclassified raster, merging cells of the same class
dem_polys <- sf::st_as_sf(dem_rcl, merge = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(dem.tif) %>%
  summarise() # Dissolve into one (multi)polygon per class

# Compute the mean of DEM values falling inside each polygon
aggregate(dem, by = dem_polys, FUN = mean) %>%
  sf::st_as_sf() %>%
  mutate(cats = dem_polys$dem.tif)
```

## Explore NDVI and NDWI at Zion National Park

```{r}
scale_factor <- 0.0000275
offset <- 0.2

# Arithmetic on a stars object is applied to every grid cell
landsat_scaled <- landsat * scale_factor + offset

ndwi_fun <- function(green, nir){
    (green - nir)/(green + nir)
}

ndvi_fun <- function(nir, red){
  (nir - red)/(nir + red)
}

# Split the "band" dimension into attributes (X1 = blue, X2 = green, X3 = red, X4 = NIR)
landsat_bands <- split(landsat_scaled, "band")
landsat_bands

ndwi_rast <- landsat_bands %>%
  transmute(ndwi = ndwi_fun(green = X2, nir = X4))

ndvi_rast <- landsat_bands %>%
  transmute(ndvi = ndvi_fun(nir = X4, red = X3))

plot(ndwi_rast,
     main = "Zion National Park NDWI")

plot(ndvi_rast,
     main = "Zion National Park NDVI")

combine <- c(ndvi_rast, ndwi_rast) # Combine as two attributes

plot(merge(combine)) # Merge attributes into a dimension to plot side by side

# Calculate correlation between the two attributes
cor(as.vector(combine$ndvi), as.vector(combine$ndwi), use = "complete.obs")
```

## Change resolution of elevation at Zion National Park 


```{r}
plot(srtm)

# Create empty template from the bounding box of srtm
rast_template <- stars::st_as_stars(sf::st_bbox(srtm), dx = 0.01, dy = 0.01)

# use_gdal = TRUE is needed for methods other than nearest neighbor
srtm_resampl1 <- stars::st_warp(srtm, dest = rast_template, method = "bilinear", use_gdal = TRUE, no_data_value = -9999)
srtm_resampl2 <- stars::st_warp(srtm, dest = rast_template, method = "near", use_gdal = TRUE, no_data_value = -9999)
srtm_resampl3 <- stars::st_warp(srtm, dest = rast_template, method = "cubic", use_gdal = TRUE, no_data_value = -9999)
srtm_resampl4 <- stars::st_warp(srtm, dest = rast_template, method = "cubicspline", use_gdal = TRUE, no_data_value = -9999)
srtm_resampl5 <- stars::st_warp(srtm, dest = rast_template, method = "lanczos", use_gdal = TRUE, no_data_value = -9999)

srtm_resampl_all <- c(srtm_resampl1, srtm_resampl2, srtm_resampl3, srtm_resampl4, srtm_resampl5)
names(srtm_resampl_all) <- c("Bilinear", "Near", "Cubic", "Cubic Spline", "Lanczos")

plot(merge(srtm_resampl_all))
```


## terra vs. stars: what’s the difference?
Note: The written comparison below is based on Chapter 7: Introduction to sf and stars in Spatial Data Science: With Applications in R by Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand.

Both packages gave the same answers above (identical class means and an NDVI–NDWI correlation of about -0.91). The difference is in how each package represents raster data.

### terra (successor of raster)

- raster, and now its successor terra, has long been the main R package for powerful, flexible, and scalable raster analysis.
- Its data model is a 2D regular raster, or a set (stack) of raster layers. This fits a static “GIS view” of the world, where each theme is a layer.
- For data that change over time, a layer stack means the user has to keep track of which layer represents what (e.g., which layer is which date or band).

### stars (spatiotemporal arrays)

- stars was written to support raster and vector data cubes. Raster layers, raster stacks, and feature time series are special cases of a data cube.
- A stars object is a list of arrays (attributes) plus a table of dimensions (x, y, band, time, …) with fields like offset, delta, and refsys. Time is just another dimension, so time-varying raster stacks are represented directly.
- It handles regular grids as well as rotated, sheared, rectilinear, and curvilinear rasters, and arrays whose spatial dimension is a set of geometries (vector data cubes).
- It is tightly integrated with sf: functions share the st_ prefix, rasters can be cropped or aggregated with sf objects, and st_as_sf() converts back to sf.
- It follows tidyverse design: filter(), slice(), mutate(), and transmute() work on data cubes.
- It aims to scale beyond local disk size; stars_proxy objects are essentially pointers to files that are only read when needed.
